title: on_commit lambdas close over the loop-local pr_url instead of a bound snapshot
body: Both new on_commit lambdas capture the function-local `pr_url` by closure, but Django runs them later, at transaction commit. The new code works around this only for the stamphog leg, with `stamphog_pr_url = pr_url` on line 130 and a closure over that copy. The pre-existing `_start_review` lambda right above (lines 116-125) still closes over `pr_url` directly, so this chunk ships two different closure conventions for the same value in adjacent blocks. The dedicated copy is a readability fix, not a real guard: a later `pr_url = ...` rebinding would still be picked up through the closure. Only binding the value as a lambda default (`lambda pr_url=pr_url: ...`) or using `functools.partial` actually snapshots it at registration time. Note `ReviewUserSettings.load(...)` (line 114) also runs synchronously inside the receiver now — a new per-save DB read on the hot TaskRun save path — though that is a reliability call for another perspective.

title: SignalImplementationRunDTO declares UUID fields but every consumer stringifies them — contract does not match usage
body: `SignalImplementationRunDTO` is declared with pydantic `UUID` types for `run_id`, `task_id`, and `signal_report_id`, and the docstring calls these "identity facts" for cross-product consumers. But the only consumer in this chunk (`_inbox_rereview_carve_out` in stamphog's tasks.py, lines 206–215) immediately stringifies all three (`str(run.signal_report_id)`, `str(run.run_id)`), and the inbox provenance blob persisted on `ReviewRun.output["inbox_review"]` stores plain strings. Meanwhile review_hog's resolver signature (`InboxActingReviewerResolver = Callable[[int, str, int | None], int | None]`) takes `signal_report_id` as `str`. The result is three different representations of the same identity (ORM UUID → pydantic UUID → str) crossing two facade boundaries, and the DTO type annotation advertises a contract no caller relies on. Pydantic's runtime validation will also coerce a UUID-shaped string back into `UUID`, so a future caller passing the receiver's string form would silently get a different type than the annotation suggests.

title: Inbox acting-reviewer hook accepts signal_report_id as str with no team-scoped re-validation of the report itself
body: The registered resolver contract is `(team_id, signal_report_id: str, task_created_by_id) -> int | None`. The implementation in review_hog (`resolve_stamphog_acting_reviewer` → `_resolve_assigned_reviewer`) filters `SignalReportArtefact` by `team_id` + `report_id`, so the artefact lookup is team-scoped — good. But nothing in the chain validates that `signal_report_id` is well-formed: it arrives from `str(task.signal_report_id)` (an FK id, safe today) yet the hook's public contract accepts any string from any registered caller, and a non-UUID string would silently miss the artefact and return None (fail closed, so no privilege gain) while logging nothing. Since this hook is the security gate that replaces author trust for the bot-author carve-out, a malformed-id failure mode that fails silently makes toggle regressions hard to distinguish from "no reviewers resolved".

title: Approval rationale lost when PR flips from draft to ready (case the PR says does nothing)
body: With self_driving set, the draft prerequisite is skipped, so stamphog posts a GitHub approval on a draft PR and its verdict comment says the PR is safe to merge. The PR description states that 'draft becomes ready' deliberately does nothing, so no re-review runs when the PR flips to ready. A human who filters their queue to ready PRs, or the merge-queue itself, then sees an approved PR with no comment at ready-for-review time explaining that the approval was granted against a draft on a bot author under the inbox carve-out. The same holds for new commits: the approval is dismissed and re-reviewed, but the ready-flip path reuses the draft-time approval with no fresh rationale.

title: has_reviewable_repo_config does not filter provider='github'
body: has_reviewable_repo_config counts any enabled, synced config as making the inbox toggle actionable, but process_inbox_pr_review (the task the toggle ultimately drives) resolves its config with provider='github' (tasks.py line 1143). The model documents GitHub as the only implemented provider today, so this is latent rather than live: the moment a second provider is added, the UI toggle renders enabled for teams whose only configs the review task will silently no-op on, contradicting the docstring's 'hosted reviews can actually run on'.

title: self_driving_review flag is coerced with bool() instead of checked strictly
body: bool(context.get('self_driving_review')) treats any truthy JSON value as opting into the carve-out — including a string like "false", a number, or a non-empty list. The hosted server stamps a real boolean (bool(output.get('inbox_review')) in activities.py), so this is not reachable through the normal producer, and the context file is server-provisioned rather than attacker-controllable. But this flag is the single switch that relaxes the bot-author refusal and the draft prerequisite, so a loose truthiness coercion is a weak guard for a gate this sensitive: a malformed or hand-assembled context would fail open instead of closed.

title: Toggle re-resolution on every carved-out delivery costs several uncached queries per synchronize
body: For a positively identified self-driving PR, every synchronize / reopened / base-retarget delivery runs the full resolution chain: _resolve_repo_config (1 query), find_signal_implementation_run → find_task_run (pr_url leg is index-backed, good), then the registered resolver — which in review_hog's receivers.py performs the SignalReportArtefact query, resolve_org_github_login_to_users, and ReviewUserSettings.load. A bot pushing fix commits in quick succession (or GitHub fan-out redelivering) multiplies this chain per delivery. The webhook path already recognizes this pattern for a similar per-delivery lookup: _author_lacks_write_permission caches its GitHub answer for 60s to absorb synchronize bursts.

title: Inbox re-review after a base retarget leaves the old-head approval standing on the new base
body: A base retarget arrives as action `edited` and takes the base_retargeted path: `_retract_approvals_on_base_retarget` dismisses the standing approval because every head-keyed sweep is blind to a same-head approval over a changed diff (comment at lines 831-834). For a self-driving PR whose acting reviewer is opted in, the carve-out then resolves and the delivery continues into the create path. The new run is created with the SAME head_sha as the still-current run (a retarget does not move the head), so `_supersede_prior_runs` cancels it and the fresh review proceeds — correct. But the ordering is wrong for this one case: the explicit retraction at lines 853-862 already dismissed the approval, while the replacement review only posts its verdict minutes later, after the sandbox run completes. For a carved-out inbox PR this is a deliberate double-review trigger the PR description lists as a re-review case (Case: base retarget), yet unlike every other re-review path there is no approval continuity: between retraction and the new verdict the PR sits with zero stamphog approval even though nothing about the head changed and the prior verdict was for the same commits. If the retargeted base makes the diff identical (retargeting between two bases at the same tree, or a retarget followed by a retarget back), the sandbox spend and the approval gap buy nothing. The human-PR path accepts this because a retarget genuinely changes the reviewed diff; the inbox path inherits it without anyone checking whether the retarget actually changed the diff the engine will see (base_sha is part of the engine context, so the new review does see the new base — the gap is only the missing dedupe against an unchanged effective diff and the approval-less window).

title: register_inbox_acting_reviewer_resolver silently overwrites any previously registered resolver
body: The registry is a single module-level global with last-write-wins semantics and no guard. Today only review_hog's `connect()` registers, and `AppConfig.ready()` runs once per process, so this is latent. But the module's own docstring frames it as a general inversion-hook registry (mirroring managed_viewset_hooks), and nothing enforces the single-registrant invariant: a second product registering a resolver — or a test module that registers a stub and another that re-registers — silently replaces the toggle gate for every webhook carve-out resolution in the process. Because the resolved acting reviewer gates whether a bot-authored draft bypasses the author-trust pre-filters, a wrong resolver registered later (e.g. one that resolves a different user's settings row, or a test double that always returns a user id) would apply the wrong person's toggle to live re-review decisions with no error anywhere. The failure mode is silent and security-relevant for the same reason the carve-out itself is: this hook replaces author trust for the bot-author path.

title: AGENTS.md carve-out section has the same em-dash and density problem
body: The new section uses em dashes throughout ("refused at every layer — the webhook pre-filter ... and the Action's job gates — with ONE deliberate exception", "relaxes exactly two gates — the bot-author refusal and the draft prerequisite ... — and swaps human-author trust context"). AGENTS.md is agent-facing, but the same file's older sections ("The stale-approval invariant", "Trust boundaries") mostly avoid em dashes, so the new section also breaks the file's own style. The first bullet's "It relaxes exactly two gates ... and swaps human-author trust context for a TRUSTED provenance block" sentence packs three claims into one line, and a reader must hold all three to act on any one.

title: process_inbox_pr_review can restart a stranded inbox run after the toggle was switched off
body: The head-keyed dedupe treats a still-QUEUED run as "restart it" without re-checking anything. Two cases matter. (1) The existing QUEUED run is an inbox run (created by this task with `output["inbox_review"]`): the receiver re-fires on every TaskRun output save, so a later save restarts the workflow even if the acting reviewer switched `stamphog_review_inbox_prs` off in the meantime. The restart path never calls `get_inbox_acting_reviewer_resolver()`, so Case 3 in the PR description ("everyone turns the toggle off, mid-PR") is only honored for brand-new heads, not for this restart path. (2) The existing QUEUED run is a plain webhook run (no inbox provenance): a receiver refire restarts it and returns early, so a missed/lost `synchronize` delivery for that head would NOT get the inbox review the docstring promises ("a refire after a head the webhook leg never delivered still reviews the new commits") — the dedupe key is (pull_request, head_sha) regardless of provenance. Note the security boundary itself holds: the engine keys off persisted provenance, so case (2) never gains self-driving privileges; the concern is the toggle contract and the documented lost-synchronize recovery.

title: Stamphog toggle can be switched on while disabledReason simultaneously blocks the switch
body:
The disabledReason expression only forces the switch disabled when `!settings.stamphog_connected && !settings.stamphog_review_inbox_prs`. When the project has no synced, enabled Stamphog repository but the user's toggle is already on, the switch falls through to `switchDisabledReason` and stays interactive — this is deliberate for opting out. The same fall-through also applies while a save is in flight: `switchDisabledReason` is `'Saving…'` whenever `settingsLoading` is true, regardless of which field the in-flight PATCH carries. That part is consistent with the neighboring switches and is fine.

The correctness gap is the opt-in direction on the backend. The UI prevents turning the toggle ON while disconnected, but nothing in `ReviewUserSettingsSerializer` enforces it: a direct PATCH to the settings endpoint with `stamphog_review_inbox_prs: true` succeeds while `stamphog_connected` is false. The stored row then says opted-in while the only enforcement of the precondition lives in a disabledReason string. The dispatch path tolerates this (the queued stamphog task no-ops without a repo config), so no review misfires — but the settings state and the UI copy ('Only takes effect when the project has a synced, enabled Stamphog repository') now disagree with what the API actually persisted, and any future consumer that trusts the toggle without re-checking the repo config inherits the inconsistency.

title: get_stamphog_connected reads a per-request cross-DB flag with no caching, inside an endpoint that also serves PATCH responses
body:
`get_stamphog_connected` runs `has_reviewable_repo_config(instance.team_id)` — an `.exists()` query against the separate stamphog product database — on every serialization of the settings object. Serialization happens on both the GET and on every PATCH response in `user_settings` (line 137 returns `serializer.data` after save), so each settings read and each toggle flip costs a cross-database round trip on the request path. The value is project-scoped, not user-scoped, and changes only when a Stamphog repo config is synced, enabled, disabled, or removed — far less often than this endpoint is hit (the Code review tab calls it on every visit, and the optimistic UI PATCHes on every switch flip).

This is a correctness-of-data-access concern rather than pure performance: the endpoint's availability and latency are now coupled to the stamphog DB on every call. The fail-soft try/except handles outright errors, but a slow (not failed) stamphog DB still adds its full latency to every settings read and every settings write response, and the circuit breaker the comment mentions only helps once it trips.

title: Receiver-leg task does not positively identify the PR as self-driving (unlike the webhook leg)
body: process_inbox_pr_review reviews any open PR URL passed to it, as long as the team has a synced+enabled StamphogRepoConfig for the parsed repository. It never checks that the PR is bot-authored, that its head is repo-native, or that it links back to the signal-implementation run it claims (no find_signal_implementation_run call, no task.repository comparison). The webhook leg (_inbox_rereview_carve_out) requires all of these before stamping the inbox provenance that turns on the engine's self_driving_review carve-out. The receiver leg trusts the caller's pr_url completely: that URL comes from TaskRun output written by the task's agent, and review_hog's receiver only checks signal_report_id / internal / the toggle — it never compares the PR URL's repo to task.repository. So if an agent records a pr_url for a different (but team-configured) repository, or for a human-authored PR in the right repo, this leg creates a run stamped with self-driving provenance for a PR the webhook leg would refuse to identify. That run bypasses the review-mode and write-permission gates downstream (inbox_review is not None), and skips the author merged-PR fetch, for a PR shape those gates were meant to govern.

title: process_inbox_pr_review can leave a run QUEUED with no workflow after the final retry
body: When the post-commit _start_review_workflow raises (Temporal down), the exception propagates into the except Exception block and retries the Celery task; the retry re-enters through the dedupe and restarts the still-QUEUED run. That recovery only works while retries remain. With max_retries=3, if the start keeps failing the task exhausts retries and the run stays QUEUED forever: unlike the webhook path there is no delivery id, no GitHub redelivery, and no later code path that re-discovers a stranded QUEUED inbox run. The next receiver refire only happens on another TaskRun output save carrying the PR URL, which may never come for this PR. The user-visible result is a self-driving PR that never gets its initial review and no error surfaced anywhere.

title: Dedupe in process_inbox_pr_review treats a GATED run at the current head as 'already reviewed'
body: The head-keyed dedupe excludes SUPERSEDED and FAILED but keeps GATED (and COMPLETED) as dedupe hits: a refire finds the GATED run at the same head and no-ops. GATED is a deterministic gate block (e.g. an active CHANGES_REQUESTED at run time), not a delivered verdict, and the gate inputs can change without the head moving (a maintainer dismisses their CHANGES_REQUESTED review). On the human path this is fine because any subsequent relevant webhook delivery creates a fresh run (GATED is terminal so it is not superseded, but a new head or label event still queues one). On the inbox path, a receiver refire is exactly the mechanism documented for recovering missed events, yet it can never re-review a same-head PR whose previous run GATED — the toggle-holder has no way to get a verdict at that head once the blocking review is dismissed.

title: Circuit-open stamphog DB outage produces a full exception log on every settings read
body: get_stamphog_connected catches every Exception from has_reviewable_repo_config and logs it with logger.exception. When the stamphog product database is down, the fail-fast circuit breaker (posthog/db_backends/failopen/base.py) raises CircuitOpenError in microseconds on each connection attempt. This endpoint runs on every Code review scene mount and again on every settings PATCH response, so an open circuit turns into one full traceback (and one error-tracking event) per page load per user for the whole outage. The fail-soft False return is correct; the per-call exception logging is the part that amplifies an outage into log and Sentry noise.

title: Disabled-toggle message reads as 'not set up' during a transient stamphog DB outage
body: stamphog_connected fails soft to False in the serializer when the stamphog database read errors. The switch then renders disabled for users whose toggle is off, with the reason 'Connect a repository to Stamphog first. Stamphog is not set up for this project yet.' During an outage that message is wrong: the project may have a connected repository, and the copy points the user at a setup flow that would not fix anything. The practical impact is small (the toggle recovers when the read recovers, and an already-on switch stays interactive), but the message actively misleads during the failure window.

title: Inbox-leg Celery retry budget is too small for the one trigger with no redelivery behind it
body: process_inbox_pr_review is decorated with max_retries=3 and default_retry_delay=5, the same budget as the webhook-leg tasks. But the task's own docstring states the difference: "the toggle-gated initial review has no webhook redelivery behind it, so a transient GitHub blip must not silently lose it." The retry policy does not match that statement. Four attempts over roughly 15 seconds covers a sub-minute blip only. A GitHub outage or secondary rate limit lasting a few minutes at PR-creation time exhausts the retries, the task raises MaxRetriesExceededError, and the initial draft-time review is permanently lost — the reviewer's re-fire depends on a later TaskRun output save, which is not guaranteed once the run is done. The PR is only reviewed again when someone pushes new commits and the webhook carve-out fires. The webhook leg does not have this problem because GitHub's own redelivery window (hours) backstops the same retry budget. The rate-limit branch (countdown=max(e.retry_after or 0, 60)) improves the rate-limited case but still caps at three retries, and secondary rate limits regularly outlast that.

title: No head-keyed dedupe between the webhook carve-out leg and a receiver refire — racing legs can both start a workflow for the same head
body: The new receiver leg (process_inbox_pr_review) dedupes on (pull_request, head_sha) before creating a run. The webhook create path does not: it dedupes on delivery_id only and supersede-then-creates on every relevant delivery. Two triggers for the same head can therefore create two QUEUED runs: e.g. a receiver refire fetches the PR and creates a run at head H while a synchronize webhook for the same head H resolves the carve-out and creates its own run at head H (the receiver's row was not yet visible, or the webhook arrived first and the receiver's dedupe only catches the reverse ordering). The second creator's _supersede_prior_runs marks the first run SUPERSEDED, but if the first run's workflow already passed the SUPERSEDED guards in run_review_in_sandbox, both sandboxes burn a full clone + LLM review for the identical head. This is a waste-of-spend race, not a correctness hole — the supersede guard and post_verdict checks contain the verdict outcome.

title: README addition uses em dashes and hedged phrasing the copy rules ban
body: The new paragraph contains six em dashes used as punctuation ("calls the `queue_inbox_pr_review` facade — gated by ... toggle on ReviewHog's settings — and the initial review runs ...", "(task linkage through the tasks facade, toggle re-checked through `facade/inbox_hooks.py`); every other bot author ..."). The project copy rules forbid em dashes in text a person reads, and the CLAUDE.md rule treats doc quality as part of the PR, not a follow-up. The paragraph is also one very long sentence that chains four clauses, so the two-leg trigger story is hard to scan.

title: README cross-reference to AGENTS.md is imprecise and omits the relative link the file uses elsewhere
body: The paragraph ends with "See AGENTS.md § the self-driving carve-out." Two problems: (1) every other reference to AGENTS.md in this file and in AGENTS.md itself uses a relative markdown link (README.md links `[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md)` in the security paragraph; AGENTS.md links `[README.md](README.md)`), and this one is plain text; (2) the section is actually titled "The self-driving inbox carve-out (the one exception to the bot-author refusal)", so "the self-driving carve-out" does not match the heading and an anchor link would not resolve.

title: Inbox carve-out bypasses the fork and author-trust gates without re-verifying that the PR author is the team's own GitHub App machine user
body: The carve-out in _inbox_rereview_carve_out admits a bot-authored PR past every trust gate (bot-author, draft, author_association, write permission, review mode) based on four checks: repo-native head, a synced+enabled repo config, a tasks-facade run match, and the acting reviewer's toggle. What it never checks is that the PR author IS the identity the self-driving flow uses. The docstring asserts "authorship is forced to the team's GitHub App machine user", but the code does not compare pr.user.login / pr.user.id against that identity. The task-facade match is by pr_url or by (repository, head_branch) — both are branch-name or URL strings that any GitHub App installed on the same repository (or any bot given a colliding branch name on a branch the tasks product also pushed, e.g. a resumed/shared work branch) could satisfy. find_task_run's branch leg matches ANY non-wizard TaskRun with that branch on that repo, including a run whose PR was opened by a different bot on the same branch. If another bot (or a compromised automation with push access to a branch a signals run used) opens a PR whose head branch still matches a signal-report task, this function returns provenance, and the delivery then sails past bot_author/draft/association/write-permission gates and gets a head-pinned auto-approval. Positive identification of a self-driving PR should include the author identity, not just repo+branch linkage.

title: _parse_pr_url matches github.com anywhere in the string and accepts extra path segments, so a crafted or malformed URL can bind the wrong repo
body: _PR_URL_RE is re.search(r"github\.com/([^/\s]+/[^/\s]+)/pull/(\d+)") with no host anchor and no end anchor. Two consequences: (1) a URL like https://evil.example/?u=github.com/acme/widgets/pull/12 parses as acme/widgets — the receiver leg would then review PR #12 of acme/widgets if the team has a config for it, while the string was never a GitHub URL for that repo; (2) the repo capture group [^/\s]+/[^/\s]+ is greedy across exactly two segments, but because there is no $ anchor after (\d+), URLs with trailing segments (pull/12/files) still match — fine — yet URLs like github.com/a/b/c/pull/12 capture b/c, silently shifting which repo gets matched. The webhook-leg caller passes GitHub's own html_url so shape is guaranteed there, but process_inbox_pr_review consumes a stored string that has already crossed a process boundary, and it is the only validation before a config lookup and a privileged review are keyed off it.

title: Base-retargeted inbox PRs proceed on a snapshot whose base differs from what was just reviewed and dismissed
body: For a base retarget (`edited` + `changes.base`), the flow is: `_retract_approvals_on_base_retarget` supersedes every non-terminal run and dismisses approvals at every head (with copy saying 'Stamphog re-reviews automatically'), then `_inbox_rereview_carve_out` admits the delivery via `base_retargeted`, then `mode_skip_reason` and the write-permission gate are bypassed, and a new run is created from the SAME payload. GitHub's `edited` payload describes the PR before the retarget is fully recomputed — `pr.base.sha` still points at the old base in this delivery. The webhook path passes this payload's `base.sha` into `build_reviewer_invocation(base_sha=...)`, so the replacement review can run against the pre-retarget diff. For human PRs in LABEL mode this wrong-base review usually doesn't happen (the trigger label is absent), but the carve-out explicitly bypasses the mode gate. The run is also head-keyed and the head didn't move, so the later `synchronize` (recompute push) finds the current head already reviewed by this run and — if the run is no longer QUEUED — does not re-review.

title: Receiver-leg dedupe restarts a stranded QUEUED run but keeps its stale provenance (acting reviewer / toggle state at first fire)
body: When a repeat receiver fire finds an existing QUEUED run at the current head, the run's workflow is restarted but its `output.inbox_review` is left as-is. That provenance was stamped from the FIRST fire's `acting_user_id` and toggle check. If the toggle was switched off (or assignment changed) between the first fire and the restart, the restarted run still executes under the stale acting reviewer — unlike the webhook path, which re-resolves the toggle on every delivery. The window is narrow (post-commit workflow-start failure plus a receiver refire), but the restart is the documented recovery path for exactly that failure, and the refire already carries fresh `acting_user_id` it doesn't use.

title: self_driving flag missing from engine-side review telemetry
body: The PR adds self_driving to the classification dict (line 477) and to the to_dict() audit trail (line 938), but _capture_review_completed (lines 815-855) does not emit it as a stamphog_self_driving property on the stamphog_review_completed event. The hosted server does stamp stamphog_self_driving_review into STAMPHOG_EXTRA_PROPERTIES (products/stamphog/backend/temporal/activities.py), which covers hosted runs through analytics_extra_properties(). Two gaps remain: (1) the engine's own event cannot show whether the flag was on for a run unless the server-side property happens to be present, so any run where the env injection fails or is absent records nothing; (2) the reliability guarantee this PR relies on - Action behavior is unchanged by construction, self_driving always False there - is not directly verifiable from the engine's telemetry, because the engine never records the value it actually used. If a future change ever set the flag on an Action run, no event would show it. For a feature whose safety story rests on default-off and on auditing which gates ran relaxed, the flag should be observable on every review event.

title: has_reviewable_repo_config counts configs whose connecting user is deactivated or deleted, so stamphog_connected renders the toggle enabled although every review fails at token minting
body: The function's docstring defines a reviewable config as one whose connecting user exists, because the sandbox LLM credential is minted under that principal. The query only checks connected_by_user_id__isnull=False. _mint_reviewer_gateway_token additionally requires User.objects.filter(pk=user_id, is_active=True) to find a row, and raises otherwise. When the user who connected the installation leaves the org or is deactivated, the config row keeps its non-null connected_by_user_id, this function keeps returning True, and the Code review scene renders the stamphog_review_inbox_prs toggle as usable. Every queued inbox review then fails closed at token minting. The failure is safe, but the UI flag is wrong in exactly the way the flag exists to prevent: the toggle has nothing to act on, yet it is not rendered disabled. Re-syncing the installation stamps a fresh connecting user, but nothing prompts that while the flag says the repo is connected.

title: Carve-out section omits the fork-safety and synced-repo identification gates
body: The section says positive identification is "a non-internal, signal-report-carrying TaskRun matched through the tasks facade", and the first rule says "Identification is task linkage, never author-login matching." The implementation in `_inbox_rereview_carve_out` (products/stamphog/backend/tasks/tasks.py) applies two more identification gates before the facade match: the PR head repo must equal the event repo (fork PRs are rejected because `head.ref` is attacker-controlled on a fork while `repository.full_name` stays the base repo, so a branch-keyed task match could bind an unrelated fork PR to a run), and the repo must resolve to a synced+enabled config (`_resolve_repo_config`, non-blank `installation_id`, `connected_by_user_id` set). The receiver leg similarly no-ops without a synced+enabled config. This file is the contract for agents: it lists the review-mode and author-write-permission gates the carve-out bypasses, but not the fork-safety gate that stops the widened exception from binding an attacker's fork PR to someone else's task run. An agent asked to widen or refactor the carve-out from this doc alone could drop a gate the doc never mentioned.

title: README says "Later pushes re-review" but the webhook leg covers reopen and base retarget too
body: "Later pushes re-review through the normal webhook path" covers only `synchronize`. The webhook carve-out (`_inbox_rereview_carve_out`) also fires on `reopened` (it is in `_HEAD_CHANGING_ACTIONS`) and on base retarget (`edited` with `changes.base`), and the AGENTS.md section added in the same chunk says "synchronize / reopen / base retarget". A reader of the README could conclude that a close-and-reopen cycle or a base change on a carved-out PR leaves the approval stale, when the code re-reviews those events too. The README and AGENTS.md now disagree on the same trigger set.

title: Initial Stamphog inbox review trusts an unverified agent-written pr_url, bypassing every approval gate
body: The receiver reads pr_url from TaskRun.output — a field written by the agent server from observing an LLM agent's actions — and forwards it to stamphog's queue_inbox_pr_review with no check that the URL's repository matches task.repository (repository is already parsed and in scope at line 106, but only used for the branch leg). On the stamphog side, process_inbox_pr_review (the task this dispatches to) stamps inbox_review provenance unconditionally once the team has any synced+enabled StamphogRepoConfig for the URL's repo: it never verifies the PR is bot-authored, never calls find_signal_implementation_run, and never cross-checks signal_report_id or task_run_id. The engine's self-driving carve-out then keys off that provenance alone, so the run skips the bot-author, draft, author-association, and write-permission gates that protect every other stamphog path, and an approve-first review posts a real GitHub approval that can satisfy branch protection. The webhook re-review leg does this identification rigorously (_inbox_rereview_carve_out: bot author, fork check, find_signal_implementation_run match, team recheck); the initial leg does none of it. The PR description states 'a background job checks the PR is really ours (our bot, no fork, the task's repo)' — that check is absent on this leg. Concrete failure: a signals task whose agent is prompt-injected (or simply errs) into recording a human-authored PR URL from the same configured repo in output.pr_url gets that PR an approval-capable review, with the approval attributed to the opted-in acting reviewer.

title: Stamphog toggle is checked only at dispatch time; the queued task never re-checks it before minting an approval
body: settings.stamphog_review_inbox_prs is read once in the receiver and the result is baked into the on_commit dispatch. The facade contract ('the caller has already resolved the acting reviewer and checked their stamphog_review_inbox_prs toggle') makes the queued task trust that snapshot. Unlike the webhook re-review leg — which re-checks the toggle on every delivery through resolve_stamphog_acting_reviewer — the initial review has no re-check at execution time. A user who switches the toggle off in the seconds between the TaskRun save and the Celery task running still gets a Stamphog review and a potential GitHub approval on their PR. The window is small (broker latency), but the initial leg is also the only one with no webhook redelivery behind it, so a stale read is never corrected. The stale-approval dismissal machinery only fires on later head-changing webhook events, so an approval minted from a stale toggle read can stand if no push follows.

title: Branch-leg task match in find_signal_implementation_run is not scoped to non-terminal runs, so a stale branch name can re-identify a PR as self-driving after the run ended
body: find_signal_implementation_run delegates to webhooks.find_task_run. The pr_url leg prefers non-terminal runs but falls back to terminal ones by design (post-merge handling). The branch leg (TaskRun.objects.filter(branch=branch, task__repository__iexact=repository, state__wizard_head_branch__isnull=True).first()) has no terminal-status exclusion and no created-ordering guarantee beyond the default. That is correct for the webhook backstop's purpose, but this facade's caller is a security gate: the stamphog carve-out uses the match to bypass bot/draft/association/write-permission refusals and mint approvals. A PR whose head branch collides with a long-finished (or failed) signal-report task's branch on the same repo still resolves to a DTO here, and the carve-out then only asks whether SOME assigned reviewer is opted in — a preference, not an identity. Positive identification for a trust-gate bypass should bind to the live (or at least recent) run that actually produced the PR, not to any historical run that ever used the branch name.

title: Stamphog initial review is gated on the same single acting reviewer as the ReviewHog review, so an opted-in assignee gets no stamphog review when the acting reviewer is someone else
body: The PR description states the gate is "at least one of the assigned users has stamphog_review_inbox_prs enabled". The implementation checks the toggle on one user only. `_resolve_assigned_reviewer` collapses the resolved reviewer list to a single acting reviewer (the task creator if they are assigned, else the first resolved reviewer), and `settings.stamphog_review_inbox_prs` is read from that one row. If the acting reviewer has the toggle off but another assigned reviewer has it on, no stamphog review is queued. The same shape applies to the webhook leg: `resolve_stamphog_acting_reviewer` re-checks only that one user's toggle, so after the acting reviewer opts out mid-PR, re-reviews stop even if a second assignee is still opted in. The two toggles are also now coupled through the shared acting-reviewer resolution: a user who wants only the stamphog review (stamphog on, review_inbox_prs off) still blocks both reviews whenever they are the resolved acting reviewer. That may be a deliberate simplification (the ReviewHog run needs a single option snapshot, and the docstring at lines 169-172 describes toggles gating 'the respective reviews' for the acting reviewer), but it does not match the 'at least one of the assigned users' behavior the PR announces, and the mismatch is invisible to users who opted in and get nothing.

title: stamphog_connected reads the stamphog product DB with the default reader connection, unlike the writer-pinned reads used on stamphog's own gating paths
body: `get_stamphog_connected` calls `has_reviewable_repo_config(instance.team_id)`, which runs `StamphogRepoConfig.objects.for_team(team_id)...exists()` on the default (reader) connection for the stamphog database. Stamphog's own run-gating reads are writer-pinned on purpose: `process_inbox_pr_review` in products/stamphog/backend/tasks/tasks.py resolves the repo config with `.using(router.db_for_write(StamphogRepoConfig))` and comments that this is the 'writer-pinned like every read that gates run creation (reader-lag invariant)'. The case that matters here: a user syncs the Stamphog App (a write) and immediately opens the Code review settings; the GET can hit a replica that has not caught up, return `stamphog_connected: false`, and render the toggle disabled right after setup succeeded. The fail-soft `except Exception: return False` makes the same wrong answer appear on any transient read error, so the UI can show 'not connected' for a project that is connected. Impact is limited (a UI flag, and the backend re-gates the actual review on the writer DB inside the queued task, so no review is lost), so this is a consider-level observation rather than a defect.

title: Webhook path never re-checks the inbox toggle when no pre-filter trips — a toggle switched off mid-PR is ignored on ready PRs
body: The carve-out (the only place the acting reviewer's `stamphog_review_inbox_prs` toggle is re-checked on the webhook path) runs exclusively inside `if skip_reason is not None`. That guard holds for bot-authored drafts, but not for two realistic delivery shapes of a self-driving PR. (1) `ready_for_review`: the payload snapshot has `draft=False`, and since the bot's app machine user can be recorded with `author_association` MEMBER, `_review_skip_reason` can return None — the carve-out never runs, the toggle is never consulted, and the PR is re-reviewed (and potentially re-approved) even if every reviewer turned the toggle off. The head did not move, so no dismissal path fires either — the stale draft-time approval simply stays. (2) After the PR flips to ready, a `synchronize` payload also trips no pre-filter, so every subsequent push re-reviews with the toggle unchecked. Case 3 in the PR description ('everyone turns the toggle off mid-PR → no review runs') is only guaranteed while the PR remains a draft.

title: `find_task_run` branch leg can bind a PR to a run whose recorded `pr_url` points at a different PR
body: The branch-match leg of `find_task_run` filters on `branch` + repository only; it does not require `output.pr_url` to be empty or to equal the PR being identified. A resumed/retried run whose branch was reused for a second PR (the branch leg deliberately includes terminal runs) can therefore positively identify a bot-authored PR as self-driving even though that run's recorded PR URL points at a different, earlier PR number. The carve-out then stamps provenance (`signal_report_id`, `task_run_id`) from that mismatched run onto the new PR's review. The existing webhook backstop tolerates this fuzziness for follow-up events; the carve-out consumes it as a positive-identification gate, where a wrong binding mis-attributes the review and could admit a PR that no signals run actually produced.

title: Draft-gate relaxation is not coupled to the bot-authored case it was designed for
body: The self-driving carve-out is documented as covering 'a bot-authored draft PR' (see __init__ comment at lines 202-208), and every inbox PR is bot-authored by construction. But the two relaxations are applied independently: line 225 requires author_is_bot for the bot refusal, while line 590 relaxes the draft prerequisite for ANY PR whenever self_driving is set, including a human-authored one. If the hosted server ever stamps self_driving_review on a context whose PR has a human author (server bug, task-linkage confusion, a human pushing commits that flip authorship signals), stamphog would review — and on the T0 path auto-approve — a human's draft PR, exactly the case the draft prerequisite exists to prevent. The Action workflow's draft gates (.github/workflows/pr-approval-agent.yml) do not cover the hosted runtime, so this engine check is the only draft guard on that path.

title: Approval on a still-draft PR carries no draft caveat in the posted verdict body
body: With the carve-out, a self-driving PR can now reach APPROVED while still in draft state, and _render_review_body() has no branch that discloses this: the prerequisites gate row renders as '✓ all clear' and no bullet mentions that the approval was granted on a draft. The to_dict() contract records self_driving for the audit trail, but a human reading the pinned GitHub approval or the verdict comment on the PR cannot tell that the draft gate ran relaxed — the outcome looks identical to an approval on a ready PR. Since the approval takes effect when the PR flips to ready, the approving-while-draft fact is material to whoever merges it.

title: stamphog_connected issues an uncached cross-DB query on every settings GET and every PATCH response
body: get_stamphog_connected calls has_reviewable_repo_config, which queries the separate stamphog product database. The serializer runs this method on every GET of the user settings endpoint (the Code review scene's always-called endpoint, so once per page load per user) and again on every PATCH response, because the viewset returns Response(serializer.data) after a save. The frontend flips each switch through its own updateSettings PATCH, so a user toggling settings generates one cross-DB read per click. The try/except handles the stamphog DB being down (fail-fast circuit breaker), but it does nothing for the stamphog DB being slow: cross-DB latency lands directly on the request path of an interactive settings page, and there is no caching or memoization anywhere on this path.

title: get_stamphog_connected catches all Exception, masking programming errors as 'disconnected'
body: The fail-soft except Exception returns False for every failure mode, including non-operational ones: a facade signature change, an import error inside the stamphog module, or a bug in the query itself all surface to the user as 'Stamphog is not set up for this project yet' with the switch disabled. The failure is logged (logger.exception), so it is not silent for operators, but the UI state is indistinguishable from the legitimate not-connected state, which makes this class of regression hard to spot from user reports and easy to miss if the log line is not alerted on.

title: Unindexed TaskRun branch/repository lookup runs on every bot-PR webhook delivery
body: find_signal_implementation_run delegates to webhooks.find_task_run, whose fallback leg filters TaskRun on branch=... and task__repository__iexact=... Neither column has an index (TaskRun.Meta.indexes covers output->pr_url, state->wizard_head_branch, created_at, task, and team/stage/task), so when the pr_url leg misses, Postgres scans posthog_task_run joined to the task table. _inbox_rereview_carve_out calls this on every bot-authored delivery for a head-changing action on a stamphog-configured repo. Dependabot and renovate PRs never match the indexed pr_url leg (their PRs are not recorded on any TaskRun), so each of their synchronize deliveries pays the full scan. TaskRun is a hot, steadily growing table, and dependabot rebase bursts fan out many synchronize events. What starts as one scan per delivery becomes repeated scans of a large table on the webhook hot path.

title: _resolve_repo_config is queried twice per skipped bot delivery
body: When skip_reason is not None, the code first calls _inbox_rereview_carve_out, which internally resolves the repo config (line 179). When the carve-out comes back empty or opted_out, the skip path calls _resolve_repo_config(installation_id, repo) again (line 891) to run the approval retraction. That is a second identical writer-pinned query per delivery. This path runs for every bot-authored or draft PR synchronize on a configured repo, which is the common case for repos with dependabot or renovate enabled, so the duplicate query is on a hot path.

title: Each receiver refire costs a GitHub get_pr call before the dedupe can no-op
body: review_hog's receiver re-fires queue_inbox_pr_review on every TaskRun output save that carries the PR URL. process_inbox_pr_review fetches the PR from GitHub before the head-keyed dedupe, because only GitHub knows the current head. An agent run that saves output repeatedly therefore spends one GitHub API call (and one Celery task execution with config resolution) per save, even when the head has not changed and the run will no-op. The installation token's hourly rate budget is shared with the review workflow itself, so a chatty agent loop eats into it.

title: Self-driving runs keep computing the bot-author familiarity signal that the prompt then discards
body: On a self-driving run, the author is a bot by construction (the carve-out exists to review bot-authored drafts). The engine still runs _maybe_compute_familiarity on the T1-agent path: on the Action path that is one gh API call plus per-file git blame/log commands over up to 30 files (familiarity.py bounds), and on the hosted path _attach_familiarity runs the same git work from the injected author_pr_numbers. The new _format_self_driving block then tells the reviewer that author familiarity, org membership, and merged-PR history carry no signal for this PR. The result is bounded but unnecessary per-run compute (git blame across the changed files) plus a familiarity block in the prompt whose meaning contradicts the provenance block next to it - a STRONG/MODERATE band for a bot (e.g. a bot whose commits were squashed into these paths before) nudges the reviewer toward leniency that the self-driving prompt explicitly says is meaningless. The pipeline already has the self_driving value at the point both familiarity hooks run.

title: stamphog_connected is an any-repository check, but the review gate is per-repository — an opted-in user in a partially connected project gets a green-lit toggle that silently never reviews
body: get_stamphog_connected returns has_reviewable_repo_config(instance.team_id), which checks whether the team has AT LEAST ONE synced, enabled StamphogRepoConfig on any repository. The actual review gate is stricter: process_inbox_pr_review (products/stamphog/backend/tasks/tasks.py) resolves a config filtered by repository__iexact for the PR's own repository and silently no-ops (stamphog_inbox_pr_repo_not_reviewable) when that repository is not configured. In a project where Stamphog is connected for repo A but the Inbox task's repository is repo B, stamphog_connected returns true, CodeReviewScene renders the 'Let Stamphog review your Inbox PRs' switch enabled, the user turns stamphog_review_inbox_prs on — and every dispatch for repo-B PRs no-ops with no signal anywhere in the UI. The only disabled-state copy covers the fully-disconnected case ('Stamphog is not set up for this project yet'), so the partially-connected case is indistinguishable from fully working. The field's own help_text ('at least one synced, enabled Stamphog repository') is technically accurate, but the UX it drives promises coverage the per-repo gate does not deliver.

title: Permanent GitHub fetch failures (404/410) burn all three retries, then the one-shot initial review is dropped with only a log line
body: The fetch failure handler retries every non-rate-limit exception with the 5-second default delay, treating all failures as transient. A 404 (PR deleted, repo renamed or made private, installation removed) and a 410 are permanent: the task burns three retry attempts over the full backoff window and then fails for good. Unlike the webhook path, there is no redelivery behind this leg, and the docstring says the verdict must land while the PR is still a draft for Inbox triage. If the PR never gets another push, nothing re-triggers the review and the only trace is a worker log line, so a self-driving PR can sit at triage with no Stamphog verdict and no signal to anyone that it was lost. The retry posture is the right default for genuine blips; the gap is that permanent failures are indistinguishable from transient ones here.

title: Repeated saves can create a GitHub API request storm
body: The receiver queues a Stamphog task for every TaskRun save that still contains `pr_url`. This also occurs when `update_fields` is absent. The queued task fetches the pull request from GitHub before it checks for an existing review. Frequent saves can consume GitHub rate limits and fill the Celery queue with duplicate work.

title: Team scope is applied after selecting a matching run
body: `find_task_run` selects one run across all teams. This facade checks `team_id` only after that selection. If another team's run wins the ordering for the same PR URL or branch, this function returns `None` even when the requested team has a valid matching run.

title: Provenance prompt can report the wrong draft state
body: The prompt always states that the PR is a draft when `self_driving` is true. The flag records Inbox provenance, not the current draft state. A later push can run after the PR becomes ready. The reviewer then receives false trusted context and can make the wrong judgment.

title: The initial review dispatch is not durable
body: The code uses `.delay()` as the only handoff. The caller catches broker errors and does not retry them. A broker outage can permanently lose the initial review.

title: The new webhook lookup can scan the TaskRun table
body: This call can use the branch lookup in `find_task_run`. That query filters on `TaskRun.branch`, but the field has no database index. The new synchronize path runs this query for each eligible bot PR event. Its cost will grow with the full TaskRun table.

title: The documented linkage rule does not match the initial review path
body: This section says both trigger paths match the TaskRun through the tasks facade. The initial receiver path does not use that facade. It validates the TaskRun in `review_hog.backend.receivers`, then passes provenance fields through `queue_inbox_pr_review`. The Stamphog task trusts those fields and stamps `ReviewRun.output["inbox_review"]` without another linkage check. This text hides an important trust boundary in a security invariant.

title: Initial inbox review trusts unverified task arguments
body: This task grants the self-driving review exemption after it checks only the team repository configuration and PR state. It does not verify the TaskRun link, signal report, acting reviewer, current toggle, bot author, or repository-native head. A stale or incorrect TaskRun `output.pr_url` can therefore start an approval-capable review for an unrelated PR in the configured repository. A user can also disable the toggle after dispatch but before this task runs, and the task still starts the review.

title: Stamphog ignores opt-ins from other assigned reviewers
body: The code selects one acting reviewer before it checks the Stamphog toggle. It skips the review when that user opted out, even if another assigned reviewer opted in. This conflicts with the stated rule that any assigned user's opt-in enables Stamphog. The webhook resolver repeats the same error, so later commits also skip reviews.

title: The privileged flag accepts non-boolean values
body: `bool()` treats every non-empty string and object as true. A malformed value such as `"false"` therefore disables the bot-author and draft gates. This flag controls an approval security boundary, so invalid input must fail closed.

title: The prompt does not enforce removal of author familiarity
body: The prompt renders `familiarity_block` before the self-driving provenance block. A self-driving classification can still contain familiarity data. The prompt then presents author history as trusted evidence while also saying that this history carries no signal. This breaks the stated trust contract and can bias the review of machine-authored code.

title: Deferred import can escape the error handler
body: The deferred import runs before the try block. An import error will escape the on-commit callback. The caller can then report a failure after the database commit succeeds.

title: Concurrent receiver tasks can create duplicate reviews
body: The row lock does not serialize calls when no matching ReviewRun exists. Concurrent receiver tasks can both create runs and start costly workflows for one head.

title: A broker failure permanently loses the initial review
body: The Celery publish is the only handoff for the initial review. The caller catches publish failures, so a broker outage can lose the review permanently.

title: Branch fallback can authorize a PR from an unrelated bot
body: The carve-out accepts every GitHub bot. It can also identify a run by its branch when the run has no saved PR URL. An unrelated bot can create a repository-native PR with the same branch name. This match bypasses the draft, author, review mode, and write-permission gates. StampHog can then approve a PR that the implementation run did not create.

title: Initial review path does not verify the documented task linkage
body: The document says that both trigger paths verify task linkage before they set `ReviewRun.output["inbox_review"]`. The webhook path calls `find_signal_implementation_run`, but `process_inbox_pr_review` trusts its IDs. It does not load `task_run_id` or verify its team, signal report, repository, or PR. A new caller of the public facade can therefore mark an unrelated bot draft as trusted self-driving work. This mark bypasses the bot, draft, review-mode, and author-permission gates.

title: Initial review trusts unverified task provenance
body: The task trusts `team_id`, `task_run_id`, `signal_report_id`, `acting_user_id`, and `pr_url`. It only checks for a repository configuration and an open PR. A forged or stale call can mark any open PR in that repository as an inbox review. This mark bypasses the bot, draft, review mode, and author permission gates. An untrusted task agent can also record an unrelated PR URL in its output. The resulting run can post an approval to code that did not come from the claimed implementation run.

title: Team scope is applied after an unscoped run selection
body: `find_task_run` searches all teams and selects one row before this facade checks `team_id`. Two teams can have tasks for the same repository, PR URL, or branch. A row from another team can win the query and cause this function to return `None`, even when the requested team has a valid run. This does not implement the documented team-scoped lookup contract.

title: The toggle check ignores other assigned reviewers
body: The PR requires a Stamphog review when any assigned reviewer opts in. This code selects one acting reviewer before it checks the toggle. If the task creator or first reviewer opts out, the code skips the review even when another assigned reviewer opts in.

title: The queued task does not recheck the review toggle
body: The task trusts the `acting_user_id` selected before the Celery message was published. A user can disable inbox reviews while the message waits in the queue. The delayed task still creates a review with self-driving provenance.
